content: Fetal movement refers to the motion of a fetus caused by its own muscle activity. Locomotor activity begins during the late embryological stage and evolves in nature throughout development. Muscles start to move as soon as they are innervated. These initial movements are not reflexive but are instead generated by self-initiated nerve impulses originating in the spinal cord. As the nervous system matures, muscles gain the ability to move in response to external stimuli. Although the heart begins to beat on the 23rd day after conception, this discussion focuses primarily on voluntary and reflex movements. Ages are described in terms of time from fertilization rather than gestational age. Movement during development First trimester Even before the fetal stage begins, a six-week-old human embryo can arch its back and neck. By seven weeks, movements in the arms and legs can be detected via ultrasound. In these early stages, limb movements occur simultaneously, but by the ninth week, they begin to move independently as the controlling neurons in the spinal cord develop. By week 11, the fetus can open its mouth and suck its fingers, and by week 12, it begins to swallow amniotic fluid. Second trimester By the twelfth week, the fetus is capable of kicking, curling its toes, and may even grasp its feet or scratch itself with its fingernails. It can also respond to touch on its skin. Starting around week 12, the thoracic diaphragm moves up and down as if the fetus were breathing, although this movement ceases around week 16 and does not resume until the third trimester. Movements such as kicking continue, and the mother typically feels fetal movement for the first time during the fifth month, an event known as quickening. Around this time, limb movements become more complex, involving joint flexing and rib movements, which aid in proper joint development. By approximately week 21, the fetus begins to establish a regular schedule of movement. The startle reflex is present in half of all fetuses by week 24 and in all fetuses by week 28. Movement becomes more restricted around this time due to the fetus's growth, which limits space for kicking or changing body position. Third trimester In later pregnancy, a complex motion known as stepping develops. This movement involves a circular bicycling motion of the legs, which helps the fetus move into a head-down position in preparation for birth. Variation in activity level Fetuses aged 14 to 18 weeks exhibit a pronounced circadian rhythm in their activity levels, which can be detected through fetal electrocardiograms and measurements of locomotor activity. During the last four to six weeks before birth, most of the fetus's kicking and jabbing movements occur while it is lightly sleeping. Monitoring fetal movement After quickening, pregnant women may choose to count the number and types of movements they feel their fetus make. This practice is informally known as a kick count. According to the American Pregnancy Association, the benefits of conducting kick counts range from providing an opportunity for the mother to bond with her baby to reducing the risk of stillbirth. Kick counts are particularly recommended in high-risk pregnancies. To perform a kick count, a woman finds a comfortable position, such as sitting upright with her back supported or lying on her left side (which maximizes blood flow to the fetus), and times how long it takes to feel at least ten movements, such as kicks, flutters, or rolls. Ideally, ten movements should be felt within two hours, although this number is often reached in a much shorter period. The results can be recorded to reveal the pattern of movement. Significant changes in this pattern can alert the woman to potential problems with her fetus, allowing her to notify her healthcare provider promptly.
